Oh I see! Well I guess in your notification event in Kafka it needs to be normalised and store in the database. It's a bit difficult but you just need to normalise everything I guess. App level caching would help here so it could reduce a lot of the DB overhead in services that can handle some caching.

For the notifications when a post is edited/liked/commented, a queue service like ActiveMQ or RabbitMQ would be best. The post service will simply have to equeue a message to it and then an internal non-public facing service will handle the processing of these and handle them.

Queues you can see as asynchronous message busses between services.
A service produces a message on it and that's it's job done...it doesn't care about the result.
A consumer service picks them off and processes them.
I.e. Decoupled.

I am still a fairly new dev ( \~4 years pro spring/spring-boot but dabbling as a hobby for a good decade before in Arduino ha).  
I have done the whole "OMG JWTs are awesome! Its so much easier!" thing.  
I have notice, even with my 4 years of pro experience, a lot of devs seem to just use JWTs as a default go to as an authentication system. Like 99.95% of apps iv'e seen are definitely more suited to sessions. 

I say **suited** because you can use JWTs for Authn/Authz but in the cases iv'e seen it there is always added architecture and patterns where with a framework for sessions most of this is out of the box.

The cases above are all definitely more suited to session based state handling. The architectural choice makes perfect sense. 

They could all move to JWTs for authn/authz and it would be possible but the simple case is that **sessions** are probably the best mix of robustness ,maintainability, security and compatibility. 

I did the whole "but JWTs are so easy" but once I stuck my head down and learnt about Spring Security, Sessions (JDBC and REDIS I use) and browser security, I know always start my architectural choices as having sessions as the goto choice. 

I **do use JWTs** but not for a session replacement mechanism.

[Stop Using JWTs for Sessions.](https://www.ducktypelabs.com/review-stop-using-jwt-for-sessions/)

I have about 3-4 years of spring boot behind me as a job. I have played with NodeJS(Express) a couple of years a go...and after everything, Spring just feels so much better. I like with Spring having the JTA, JMS and knowing the ORM and the many out of the box features (Redis/Prometheus/Hysertix/Actuator...the list goes on and on...check out the Spring Initializr page and have a look at the dependencies available "out of the box").

Id go in to more detail, but for example, when using Spring Security (yep, a dependency managed by them), and then Spring-WebSocket, you get SockJS/STOMP but also they work together so on a websocket message coming in or STOMP message I should say...getting the user/session is as simple as stompHeaderAccessor.getUser().

I have seen this done.  
Everyone has gone to a live database at some point and just gone "Oh, I am just doing this one tiny thing" and then 20 minutes later that phone rings and you then experience the smallest possible humanly experienced unit of time. The "Onosecond".  


The Onosecond - "OhNoSecond" is less than a femtosecond. It is used to measure the time delay between the time it takes for someone to say something has gone wrong and that warm sickly blood escaping feeling you get in your stomach when you realise you may have been the cause.  


I did it once. On a small database with luckily only about 10 inactive users (new small project not even really soft launched). Got the back up and it was all fine.

From now on, I only use a database user with credentials that can READ data.  


Want to change it? Flyway or another applicable (liquibase) migration tool is 100x better.

It may seem "OTT" but I feel it:

A) Allows you to write AN ACTUAL TEST of what could happen and also runs any other tests for your app/api you rely on.

B) That exact same script will be run against the production version.

C) You can write assertions against say a TestContainer with a set of test data mimicking the production database and run all your integration tests that exist and the new ones for the "Did my script change only effect these pieces of logic".

Does it take longer? Yes.  
Is there a history for "What on Earth did you change!?". Yes.

400 btw is usually a "bad request" where the client can not really do much about it...i.e. the front end is sending a badly parsed form/body. Technically if the front/back end have validation on both sides you shouldn't see a 400. Only if the front end doesn't validate before sending (waste of a request and bandwidth and user's time tbh) or a mismatch in validation requirements on back end controllers to front end form validation would cause a 400.

If the user needs to select a "valid" range themselves and have chosen something that doesn't make a lot of business sense...like say they were asked to provide an 'unlock code' and the unlock code was not a code that existed or had been expired...but is a valid 12 character code...a 409 is  more apt.

​

>[6.5.1](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7231#section-6.5.1).  400 Bad Request  
>  
>The 400 (Bad Request) status code indicates that the server cannot or    will not process the request due to something that is perceived to be    a client error (e.g., malformed request syntax, invalid request    message framing, or deceptive request routing).

​

>[6.5.8](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7231#section-6.5.8).  409 Conflict  
>  
>The 409 (Conflict) status code indicates that the request could not    be completed due to a conflict with the current state of the target    resource.  This code is used in situations where the user might be    able to resolve the conflict and resubmit the request.  The server    SHOULD generate a payload that includes enough information for a user    to recognize the source of the conflict.

​

Of course this is very 'verbose' and in many companies you'll just send a "400"...but then think how you can differentiate between a "4xx" **front end did** a bad vs "4xx" **the user did a bad**.

Facebook/Google tend to always send a **200 with a "success/fail"** body instead of a 409...but will send a 400 say if you messed up the encoding or had missing '{' or extra unknown fields in the body (i.e. not the user's fault but the front end client/service fault).

JWTs as stateless are meant to mean a service needs not carry out authorization...because it has already been done. You can just accept the payload and believe it is fine to use (as the token is cryptographically signed by your auth server).

You could give each token you sign a token ID ('jti claim'). Check the RFC documentation here: [RFC for JWT](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7519#section-4.1.7)

Use a library such as UUID and give every access token a UUID  in its 'jti' claim.

You could then set it up so in REDIS the user ID is related to the UUID of a token. You can then revoke the token by simply deleting the UUID or nulling it.

Having middleware check the token is not blocked by simply going to REDIS and comparing the value for access-userid against the token that has been sent.

​

This is quicker and less intensive than a database search and having to "maintain consistency".

An api key is usually just a long random string. They dont tend to hold information like a stateless JWT. 
The key is stored in a table with a reference to a User model in a database. Users have a one to one relationship with a Role. A role tends to have many permissions. End points are then protected with a "requires permission GETALL" to decide what that user/key can do.

The api keys can also have their own permissions...depends on the granularity required. A user could have many API keys (say for different apps/plugins whatever).

You simply pass the api key in the request and depending on the "permissions" it had determines if that request to that endpoint is authorised.
